To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
MMAC1 is a tumor suppressor gene that is frequently inactivated by mutation in human cancers.
MMAC1/ PTEN is a candidate tumor suppressor that is frequently inactivated in human cancers.
we identified a pseudogene of MM AC1 on chromosome 9 and that we found that MMAC1 alterations occur in a significant fraction of human cancer cell lines and primary tumor specimens.
In summary, our research is concerned with
identifying the genetic changes that occur in cancer cells and the genes involved in these changes.
the molecular genetic alterations that contribute to human cancers.
the molecular genetic analysis of MMAC1 and its role as a tumor suppressor gene in human cancer.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the MMAC1/ PTEN locus is a tumor suppressor gene in a variety of cancers, and that the frequency of MMAC1 alterations varies among different cancer types and among different tumor specimens of the same histological type.
MMAC1 is mutated in a significant fraction of cancers and that MMAC1 alterations may contribute to tumor development or progression in many human cancers.
MMAC1/ PTEN alterations occur at a low frequency in human tumors, with the highest incidence in glioblastomas and astrocytomas, and that these alterations are not specific to any one tumor type.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

MMAC1 is mutated in a subset of human tumors at a frequency that may approach 20%, with the highest frequency of alterations observed in glioblastomas and astrocytoma-derived cell lines, and the lowest in breast and prostate cancers and their cell lines.

the MMAC1/ PTEN gene is mutated in a substantial proportion (approximately 10-16%) of human cancer specimens, with a high frequency of mutations observed in glioblastomas, and that homozygous MMAC1 deletions are common in tumor cell lines.

the MMAC1 gene is mutated in 10% of the primary tumors and 16% of the tumor cell lines examined, but that homozygous deletion is a common event in tumor cell lines and may be an important mechanism of inactivation of MMAC1 in human cancers.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the MMAC1/ PTEN gene is mutated in many different human cancers, and that the gene may play a tumor suppressor role in many different types of cancer.
MMAC1/ PTEN mutations in primary tumors and cell lines occur in a broad range of cancer types.

the MMAC1/ PTEN tumor suppressor gene is mutated in a significant fraction of primary tumor specimens of multiple cancer types, including glioblastoma, astrocytoma (pediatric), leukemia (acute myeloid), melanoma, bladder carcinoma, breast carcinoma, prostate carcinoma, and testicular carcinoma.
